subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
intro: Every measurement carries a limit on how precisely it can be known. A reported quantity should never look more precise than the data it came from. In this lesson you will read the precision of a measuring tool, count significant figures, round to a stated accuracy, and propagate precision through arithmetic: products and quotients keep the significant figures of the least-precise factor, while sums and differences keep the least precise decimal place. You will also separate accuracy (closeness to the true value) from precision (fineness of the scale).

items.prompt: A graduated cylinder is marked in increments of $1\text{ mL}$. To what precision can you report a volume, and how should a reading of $24\text{ mL}$ be written with its uncertainty?

steps: The reading uncertainty of an instrument is half of its smallest scale division.
The smallest division here is $1\text{ mL}$, so the uncertainty is $\frac{1}{2}(1\text{ mL}) = \pm 0.5\text{ mL}$.
A reading made between marks is justified to the tenths place, so report the value as $24.0\text{ mL}$.
Attach the uncertainty: $24.0 \pm 0.5\text{ mL}$.
Reporting $\pm 1\text{ mL}$ would be the common error of using the full division instead of half of it.

items.prompt: How many significant figures are in the measurement $0.04060\text{ kg}$?

steps: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are never significant. The two zeros in $0.0\ldots$ do not count.
Start counting at the first nonzero digit, the $4$.
The embedded zero between $4$ and $6$ is significant because it sits between nonzero digits: $4, 0, 6$.
The trailing zero after the $6$ comes after the decimal point, so it is significant: it shows the measurement was read to that place.
Significant digits: $4, 0, 6, 0$, which is $4$ significant figures.

items.prompt: Round the measured length $12.847\text{ cm}$ to $3$ significant figures.

steps: Count off the first $3$ significant figures from the left: $1$, $2$, $8$.
The next digit decides the rounding. It is $4$.
Since $4 < 5$, the third kept digit stays as $8$ (round down).
Drop the remaining digits, keeping the value at the hundredths place.
The result is $12.8\text{ cm}$.

items.prompt: A rectangle is measured as $4.7\text{ cm}$ by $2.31\text{ cm}$. Report its area to the appropriate number of significant figures.

steps: Multiply the full measured values: $4.7 \times 2.31 = 10.857\text{ cm}^2$.
For multiplication, the result keeps the significant figures of the least-precise factor.
$4.7$ has $2$ significant figures; $2.31$ has $3$. The limiting factor is $4.7$ with $2$ significant figures.
Round $10.857$ to $2$ significant figures: the third digit is $8 \geq 5$, so the second digit $0$ rounds up to $1$, giving $11$.
Report the area as $11\text{ cm}^2$. Writing $10.857\text{ cm}^2$ would falsely claim $5$-figure precision.

items.prompt: Add the measured lengths $13.2\text{ cm}$ and $0.057\text{ cm}$ and report the sum to the correct precision.

steps: Add the values exactly: $13.2 + 0.057 = 13.257\text{ cm}$.
For addition, the result is reported to the least precise decimal place among the addends, not by significant figures.
$13.2$ is known only to the tenths place; $0.057$ is known to the thousandths place. The least precise is the tenths place.
Round $13.257$ to the tenths place: the digit after the tenths is $5$, so the tenths digit $2$ rounds up to $3$.
Report the sum as $13.3\text{ cm}$. Reporting $13\text{ cm}$ would wrongly apply the significant-figure rule to addition.

items.prompt: A ruler is marked in increments of $0.1\text{ cm}$. What is the reading uncertainty of a length measured with this ruler?
items.hint: The reading uncertainty is half of the smallest scale division.

steps: The smallest division is $0.1\text{ cm}$.
The reading uncertainty is half of this: $\frac{1}{2}(0.1\text{ cm}) = \pm 0.05\text{ cm}$.
So a length read with this ruler is uncertain by $\pm 0.05\text{ cm}$.

items.prompt: How many significant figures are in the measurement $0.003020\text{ s}$?
items.hint: Leading zeros do not count; embedded zeros and trailing zeros after the decimal point do count.

steps: The leading zeros in $0.00$ only place the decimal point and are not significant.
Begin counting at the first nonzero digit, $3$.
The embedded zero in $3, 0, 2$ is significant; the trailing zero after $2$ is significant because it follows the decimal point.
Significant digits: $3, 0, 2, 0$, which is $4$ significant figures.

items.prompt: Round the measured mass $5.6749\text{ g}$ to $3$ significant figures.
items.hint: Identify the first three significant figures, then look at the next digit to decide whether to round up.

steps: The first $3$ significant figures are $5$, $6$, $7$.
The next digit is $4$, and $4 < 5$, so round down (keep the $7$).
Drop the remaining digits, keeping the value to the hundredths place.
The result is $5.67\text{ g}$.

items.prompt: A strip of metal is measured as $3.05\text{ m}$ long and $0.40\text{ m}$ wide. Report the area to the appropriate number of significant figures.
items.hint: Multiply, then keep only as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest.

steps: Multiply the measured values: $3.05 \times 0.40 = 1.22\text{ m}^2$.
Count significant figures: $3.05$ has $3$, and $0.40$ has $2$ (the trailing zero after the decimal counts).
The limiting factor is $0.40$ with $2$ significant figures.
Round $1.22$ to $2$ significant figures: the third digit is $2 < 5$, so it rounds down to $1.2$.
Report the area as $1.2\text{ m}^2$.

items.prompt: Two balances each weigh an object whose true mass is $20.0\text{ g}$. Balance A reads $20.41\text{ g}$, $20.42\text{ g}$, $20.40\text{ g}$. Balance B reads $19.9\text{ g}$, $20.1\text{ g}$, $20.0\text{ g}$. Which balance is more precise, and which is more accurate?
items.hint: Precision is how tightly the readings cluster; accuracy is how close they center on the true value of $20.0\text{ g}$.

steps: Look at the spread of each set. Balance A's readings range only from $20.40$ to $20.42\text{ g}$, a very tight cluster, so A is more precise.
Balance B's readings range from $19.9$ to $20.1\text{ g}$, a wider spread, so B is less precise.
Now compare each cluster's center to the true value $20.0\text{ g}$. Balance A centers near $20.41\text{ g}$, about $0.4\text{ g}$ too high, so A is less accurate.
Balance B centers on $20.0\text{ g}$, right on the true value, so B is more accurate.
Conclusion: Balance A is more precise but less accurate; Balance B is more accurate but less precise. Tight agreement does not guarantee closeness to the true value.
solution.answer: Balance A is more precise (tightly clustered); Balance B is more accurate (centered on the true $20.0\text{ g}$).
